newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans clean up Oder villages, stop sandbagging.
newsitem.headline: Germans clean up Oder villages, stop sandbagging.

text.p: Soldiers started to clean up flood-hit villages and stopped sandbagging dikes along the Oder River in east Germany on Tuesday as water levels fell back steadily, officials said.

A flood crisis spokesman said the flood barriers were showing signs of holding and thousands of soldiers who had battled round the clock for days to reinforce dikes protecting the low-lying Oderbruch region had stopped sandbagging.

No new tears appeared in dikes overnight and water levels, which started dropping on Sunday for the first time in three weeks, were still going down, a spokesman for the state government in Potsdam said.

But local officials warned residents emergency measures would remain in place for the time being and said river levels, edging down by centimetres each day, had to drop by 1.5 metres before the worst was over, adding this could take until Friday.

"We must try to keep up work on the dikes. If the dikes broke now it would be a far worse pyschological blow to the population than at any time before," Matthias Platzeck, the environment minister in Brandenburg, told Berlin's InfoRadio.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl, briefly breaking off his annual summer holiday, was due to make a government statement in Bonn on aid for flood victims and a reconstruction plan in the wake of the Oder region's worst flooding in living memory.
The government and opposition were due to pass a joint plan in parliament on Tuesday earmarking up to 500 million marks ($270 million) of aid for the region.

While the Oderbruch area north of Frankfurt an der Oder, the largest city in the region along the Polish border, appeared to have escaped flooding, several villages south of Frankfurt still stood under water.
In the village of Ratzdorf at the confluence of the Oder and Neisse rivers a clean-up operation was in full swing and residents who had been evacuated were starting to return to their homes.
"We had nearly 6,000 tonnes of gravel in sandbags here, it was a huge amount," Ratzdorf's mayor Ute Petzel told the Berlin radio station.
"It looks chaotic. Technical aid workers and soldiers are helping to remove the sandbags from the streets. People are glad that their village is being to go back to normal again."
The Oder was swollen by the same rains that caused flooding in the Czech Republic and Poland last month claiming more than 100 lives and causing billions of dollars' worth of damage.
Germany has escaped the worst of the floods, but damage to homes, businesses and farms has been extensive.
German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said on Monday some 10,000 troops involved in securing the dikes would stay on to join clean-up efforts which had started in several villages.
The Federal Employment Office said the government would create jobs for 10,000 unemployed east Germans to help with reconstruction once the threat of flooding had subsided.
German President Roman Herzog was due to visit German villages and towns along the Oder River to oversee relief operations in the flood-stricken region. ($ = 1.863 German Marks)
